hints: Start by checking for allele A in each genotype, because the bullet points say pink pigment only appears when A is present.
Next ask if B can do anything on its own, or if it only works by intensifying the colour already made by A.
walkthrough:
Work Out What A Does Alone**
Allele A makes pink anthocyanin. Alleles a and b have no effect, and green is the default when no anthocyanin is made. So any genotype with at least one A, but no B, will be pink.

Add In The Effect Of B**
Allele B has no effect by itself. It only increases the pink made by A to red. That means you need both A and B together for red. Aabb has A but no B, so it stays pink. aaBB has B but no A, so no anthocyanin is made and spines stay green.
Final answer: Aabb - pink spines; aaBB - green spines.

hints: First work out the spine colour of each parent from its genotype, using the rules you used in (a).
List all the different gametes the AaBb parent can make when the two genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Remember the aabb parent can only make one type of gamete, so combine it with each gamete from the AaBb parent to get four offspring genotypes.
Translate each of the four offspring genotypes back into red, pink or green using the A-plus-B rule.
Count how many offspring show each colour to write the phenotypic ratio in its simplest form.
walkthrough:
Set Out Parents And Gametes**
AaBb contains both A and B, so it has red spines. aabb contains neither, so it has green spines. Because the genes are on different chromosome pairs they assort independently in meiosis, so AaBb makes four gamete types in equal numbers: $AB$, $Ab$, $aB$, $ab$. The aabb parent makes only $ab$ gametes.

Build The Four Offspring Genotypes**
Fertilisation gives four equally likely combinations: $AB + ab = AaBb$, $Ab + ab = Aabb$, $aB + ab = aaBb$, $ab + ab = aabb$.

Convert To Phenotypes And Ratio**
AaBb has A + B so red. Aabb has A without B so pink. aaBb and aabb both lack A so both green, even though one carries B. That gives 1 red : 1 pink : 2 green.

Final answer: parental phenotypes: AaBb red spines x aabb green spines; gametes: AB, Ab, aB, ab x ab; offspring genotypes: AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb; offspring phenotypes: red, pink, green, green; phenotypic ratio 1 red : 1 pink : 2 green.

hints: Compare meiosis when genes are on different chromosomes with when they sit close together on the same chromosome - what happens to independent assortment?
Think about how many gamete types the AaBb parent would now make most of the time, and what rare event could still make new combinations.
walkthrough:
Why Linkage Changes Gametes**
On different chromosomes, alleles of A/a and B/b separate independently to give four gamete types. On the same homologous pair of chromosomes they are linked, so they tend to be inherited together. The AaBb parent would then produce mainly the two parental gamete types, not four equal types.

Effect On The Ratio**
With only two main gamete types from AaBb combining with ab, you get only two main offspring phenotypic classes in an approximate 1:1 ratio, for example red and green. A very small number of the other phenotypes could still appear by rare crossing over and recombination between the loci in prophase I.
Final answer: Genes would be linked and inherited together with no independent assortment, giving only two phenotypic classes in 1:1 ratio, apart from rare recombinants formed by crossing over.
